Today is the twelfth lecture, where we will focus on exploring the coordination and collaboration issues between the electrical engineering discipline and other disciplines or stakeholders during project implementation. Although some of these topics have been touched upon in previous lessons, this lecture aims to systematically organize these key points to help everyone establish a comprehensive understanding, enabling better collaboration with various stakeholders in actual projects.

Next, we will explore the importance of coordination between different disciplines and stakeholders. The main parties requiring coordination include the client, regulatory authorities, utility companies, various professional teams, contractors, and suppliers, among others.

In engineering design and construction processes, effective professional coordination is crucial to prevent major issues. Based on my project experience, both domestic and international, poor coordination often leads to severe consequences. For instance, in a tissue factory project I participated in, inadequate interdisciplinary coordination ultimately resulted in significant losses. Moreover, design errors may trigger owner claims, which is why consulting firms typically carry insurance to mitigate such risks.

Poor on-site coordination can also spark conflicts, leading to rework or even unsolvable problems, not only delaying schedules but also substantially increasing project costs. Take a Dalian project as an example—an athlete village and service building constructed for the 4th National Paralympic Games. Due to coordination failures between structural and HVAC disciplines, an 800mm×1200mm fresh air vent opening was omitted, forcing workers to cut through the concrete walls of the already completed 30-story building. This approach not only impacted timelines and budgets but also posed potential risks to the building’s structural safety.

Effective professional coordination not only enhances design and construction quality but also ensures smooth project progression.

Key points for collaboration with Party A are as follows:

Effective professional coordination not only enhances design and construction quality but also ensures smooth project progression.

Key points for collaboration with Party A are as follows:

First, since Party A bears the costs, the Scope of Work must be clearly defined in the contract. Internationally, relevant documents include the RFP (Request for Proposal), RFQ (Request for Quotation), and the final signed contract. Before commencing design work, confirm the design scope thoroughly. Any ambiguities must be clarified with Party A to prevent disputes or omissions later.

For renovation projects, conduct on-site surveys and coordinate specific schedules with Party A. Additionally, request Existing Technical Documents from Party A, including drawings, specifications, operation & maintenance manuals, and technical records of all upgrades since project completion.

Regarding technical documentation, we need to clearly identify all stakeholders involved in the project, specifically the contact information of the project team. If the project is not under a general contracting model—for instance, architectural firms and engineering firms are typically separate entities overseas, with even engineering disciplines being highly specialized (e.g., independent structural engineering practices)—companies like vivo, as large enterprises, cover multiple professional domains. In contrast, small and medium-sized firms often focus on a single discipline, such as certain large-scale MEP design firms that specialize solely in mechanical and electrical engineering, excluding structural or architectural design.

During initial project meetings, all parties introduce themselves, but close collaboration with the client is necessary to obtain relevant information. On the technical side, it is essential to request the client’s Technical Specification, which is particularly common in industrial sectors. Large enterprises such as oil, power, or mining companies typically have their own design standards, developed based on universal codes while incorporating their specific requirements. When executing such projects, these standards can be directly followed, as they already encompass foundational norms. These companies maintain dedicated teams that update these standards every three years; such teams are referred to as SMEs (Subject Matter Experts).

Before starting the design, we need to coordinate with the client to clarify the project’s specific technical requirements, i.e., confirm the detailed design criteria. Below are the key points to consider:

For residential or office projects, it is necessary to specify whether appliances will use natural gas (Gas) or electricity (Electric). This primarily involves the selection of kitchen stoves, washing machines, dryers, and water heaters, which will directly impact the load calculation.

When designing large corporate or government office buildings, it is essential to understand the IT load, especially large-scale IT loads in data centers. This information is critical for system design and load calculation. The client must clarify the location, size, and required power type (normal or emergency power) for these loads.

The selection of the HVAC system is not only determined by mechanical engineering but also involves cost considerations. The client may decide on a specific type of HVAC system. During the preliminary design phase, the type of HVAC system must be confirmed with the client, as there are various heating and cooling equipment and systems available. Based on experience and discussions with mechanical engineers, the electrical power required for the HVAC system will serve as the basis for load calculations.

Additionally, it is necessary to confirm the lighting type (e.g., LED or fluorescent—currently, LED is mainstream) and its control method (e.g., occupancy sensors or centralized building control). The requirements for the security system must also be clarified, including the placement of cameras and access control systems.

In terms of equipment selection, it is necessary to coordinate with the client regarding which manufacturer’s products to adopt. For example, in building design, it is essential to clarify which areas require access control systems and which need alarm devices, all of which must be confirmed with the client regarding their specific requirements. The client typically also has an operations and maintenance (O&M) team. After the building is completed, the operation of the entire electromechanical system will be handed over to the O&M team for management. Based on their operational experience, this team may propose relevant requirements, and as design consultants, we need to consider these factors during the design phase.

The equipment provided by the client requires power supply support. A detailed equipment list must be obtained, including parameters such as power (kW/HP), single-phase or three-phase power supply, voltage, and installation locations. For long-lead items, particularly those affected by COVID-19-related supply chain delays, pre-purchasing may be required before design finalization to avoid schedule impacts. Once the system framework is established, manuals and specifications for these pre-purchased items must be promptly obtained to enable the client to place orders in advance.

In recent years, the demand for electric vehicle (EV) charging has been growing. The number of charging stations and EV parking spaces in the building also needs to be specified by the client. In North America, relevant regulations are well-established, and the design must comply with current codes and standards. If local regulations have not yet been issued, the client’s requirements will serve as the design basis. The above are the key items that need to be coordinated with the client during the preliminary design phase.

In practice, one of the primary tasks in coordinating with the client is participating in design review meetings for each milestone and deliverable. After winning the bid, the client will review the design documents and provide feedback. The responsibility is to coordinate the meeting schedule with the client and chair the design review meetings.

During the meetings, meeting minutes are prepared and written responses are provided to review comments, specifying which suggestions will be incorporated in the next submission, which have been acknowledged, and which cannot be followed due to specific reasons. After multiple rounds of communication, the final documents are confirmed and submitted. At each design stage (e.g., iFT or iFC phase), design documents are submitted to the Client.

Additionally, coordination with the Client includes project management and financial matters. For example, during the design process, the Client may request temporary additions or reductions to the design scope (design change order processing). The impact of these changes on the workload is assessed, and quotations are provided for the Client’s approval. At each design stage, invoices are issued to the Client based on the completed workload.

During the tender phase coordination, as a pure design consultant, we mainly assist the Client in the following three tasks:

1. During the bidding process, bidders may raise questions (RFIs) after reviewing the technical documents. These questions are typically submitted directly to the Client. We are responsible for answering these questions and forwarding the responses to the Client, who then shares them with the bidders.

2. If the questions involve significant design modifications or updates, further processing is required.

We need to elaborate on the legal document called addendum, which refers to officially issued drawings or written materials related to the FT (technical documents used by bidders). Modifications to the FT will form an addendum, and there may be one or multiple addenda. The final addendum, together with the FT, serves as the basis for the contractor’s bid. As part of the tender documents, the addendum also carries legal validity.

After the bidding process concludes, each contractor submits their quotation. The client typically forwards the bid packages to us, the consultants, for bid evaluation. We are required to assess each contractor from technical qualification perspectives and provide recommendations. Although the final decision on contractor selection rests with the client, bid evaluations are more common in government projects, and usually, no formal evaluation letter needs to be submitted.

During the construction phase, there is frequent coordination required with the client. As an Electrical Consultant and Electrical Contractor, the key coordination tasks include:

The chairing of construction meetings depends on the contract terms agreed with the client—it may be led by either the client or the consultant. The meeting frequency varies based on project needs, potentially weekly, biweekly, or monthly.

The chairing of construction meetings depends on the contract terms agreed with the client—it may be led by either the client or the consultant. The meeting frequency varies based on project needs, potentially weekly, biweekly, or monthly.

The contractor is responsible for submitting construction drawings, while the consultant reviews them. On-site construction may involve changes, such as issues raised by the contractor, modifications requested by the client, or design flaws identified by the consultant. These changes are referred to as Site Instructions (SI).

Site Instructions may sometimes trigger a Change Order (CO). If the change involves scope adjustments, a Change Order must be issued; otherwise, a Contemplated Change Notice (CCN) may suffice. The CCN is a preliminary document issued by the consultant, requiring the contractor to provide a quotation for review. The consultant must complete these tasks during the construction process.

If a Change Construction Notice (CCN) is issued, the contractor will submit a quotation after review. This quotation will ultimately be submitted to the consultant for evaluation to assess its reasonableness. This is one of our responsibilities as electrical consultants during the construction phase—reviewing the reasonableness of change quotations.

Payments during the construction phase are typically settled monthly. The contractor submits an invoice to the owner each month, which the owner then forwards to the consultant for review. The invoice must specify the work completed during the month and provide detailed breakdowns of material procurement costs and construction progress, such as the number of lighting fixtures installed or the progress of pipeline installation. If the consultant identifies discrepancies between the reported progress and actual progress—such as reporting 50% completion when only 30% is achieved—they must raise objections. In such cases, the consultant must conduct on-site verification to ensure the accuracy of the review.

The consultant is also responsible for conducting on-site inspections, covering both progress and quality. Inspection reports must be submitted to the owner to keep them informed of the project’s status. In practice, the consultant assumes some supervisory responsibilities during the construction phase. In North America, this role is referred to as “construction administration.” Some projects may also hire an additional “construction management team.” In the current domestic context, the role of a supervisor is equivalent to the consultant’s construction administration duties combined with the work of a construction management team.

As the project nears completion, testing and commissioning are required.

As the project nears completion, testing and commissioning are required.

As a consulting engineer, it is necessary to be on-site to supervise the commissioning process. In North America, the consulting engineer serves as the overall technical lead for the project and must be involved throughout the entire technical service process, from design to final handover. During commissioning, they must monitor progress, check for issues or fraudulent practices. Upon completion, the commissioning agent or contractor must submit test results or commissioning reports for review.

When the project is substantially complete and ready for use, despite minor outstanding issues, it is referred to as “substantial completion”. The consulting engineer must issue a “Certificate of Substantial Completion”, a critical legal document indicating the project is functionally complete. This certificate is accompanied by a “punch list” detailing the remaining minor issues to be resolved.

The “Certificate of Substantial Completion” is vital for the owner, as it can be used to apply for an “occupancy permit” from municipal authorities, confirming the project is ready for use. For contractors, this certificate is equally important—under the construction contract, it allows them to receive full payment (minus a 10% retention for warranty). The warranty period typically begins from the substantial completion date, covering equipment warranties of one, three, or five years.

This document must be stamped and certified by a Professional Engineer (P.E.). The engineer holds significant authority at this stage; if unsatisfied with the project’s completion status, they can refuse to issue the certificate, which would delay the owner’s occupancy permit and the contractor’s payment. These are the key points regarding the commissioning phase.

How do we coordinate with Party A?

How do we coordinate with Party A?

I will specifically address issues during the debugging phase in Lecture 14.

The Close-out phase primarily involves project completion coordination. As consultants, we are responsible for reviewing the O&M package, a critical technical document also referred to as the turnover package. All relevant technical documents, drawings, and specifications must be compiled into this package according to a detailed checklist. The consultant reviews and approves it; if incomplete or problematic, the contractor may be required to resubmit.

During project close-out, the contractor must also prepare the O&M package. The specific technical documents included depend on the consultant’s project requirements. For red-line as-built drawings or CAD-format drawings, our involvement is also required: any modifications during the project must be marked in red on the IFC drawings, ultimately forming the as-built drawings. Whether hard copies or electronic versions are prepared depends on the contract—either the consultant or the contractor may be responsible.

Regarding MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing) disciplines, when the entire project completes commissioning and is ready for operation, the commissioning agent, owner, or equipment supplier (e.g., Honeywell) provides training for the end-user’s operations team. While consultant participation is not mandatory, coordination with the owner or contractor may be needed for training arrangements.

The above outlines coordination and collaboration with the owner.

The above outlines coordination and collaboration with the owner.

Then I’ll continue with the explanation. Feel free to ask questions at any time.

Next, we will discuss how to coordinate with the power company. For electrical engineering, this primarily involves two aspects: high-voltage power (Power) and low-voltage communication (Communication), with more coordination work required for high-voltage power.

The first step is to determine the service size, which must be based on load calculations. During the preliminary design phase, load calculations should be as accurate as possible to avoid significant discrepancies. For example, if the initial estimate is 1000A but later increases to 3000A during the construction drawing phase, serious issues may arise. Therefore, during preliminary load calculations, appropriate allowances should be made to prevent major changes later.

After determining the service size, the power supply method—whether overhead or underground—must be decided. This requires coordination with the local power utility to understand their specific requirements and reach an agreement based on mutual needs, ultimately finalizing the incoming line method.

Additionally, the ownership of the substation must be clarified: who will build it, who owns it, and who will design and construct it. For example, in North America, some substations are designed and constructed by the power utility, while customer-owned substations inside buildings are designed by electrical consultants and built by electrical contractors.

When coordinating with the power utility, it’s also important to note that some projects may not have substations but only transformers. These transformers are typically provided by the power utility, but their installation locations must be coordinated between the electrical consultant and the power company. For substations provided by the power utility, their locations must also be coordinated. Furthermore, the location of electrical rooms inside the building and the incoming line method must be negotiated with the power company, especially for large projects (directly connected to substations) and medium-sized projects.

He may need to directly connect the utility incoming line to the meter. The meter’s location must comply with relevant standard requirements, all of which need to be considered. Regarding the specific technical requirements for metering devices, such as the configuration of CT/PT, whether to use a smart meter, master meter, or temporary meter, these are all construction-related. Temporary meters are primarily used for construction power during the construction phase, not for permit power (permanent power supply). If permanent power is already installed and available, permit power can be used. The metering during the construction phase and post-construction metering issues need to be coordinated and communicated with the utility company.

Additionally, protection coordination must be considered. Each utility company has specific requirements for protection coordination, and it is essential to ensure the system aligns with the utility’s protection scheme. When conducting power studies, especially for short-circuit current calculations, protection coordination, and arc flash analysis, the utility company must provide short-circuit capacity data as the basis for the study.

For the routing planning of primary and secondary feeders, the layout of on-site structures and underground utilities such as water, gas, and electrical lines must be considered. If underground installation is adopted, proximity to other utilities must be avoided. The utility company has specific requirements, such as maintaining a minimum distance of three feet from gas or water pipelines. During the coordination phase, a preliminary plan (side plan) will be provided, clarifying the routing within the project scope, while routing outside the project scope will be determined by the utility company.

If a cross-conflict is identified at a certain location and avoidance is desired, the path can be adjusted. The other party may raise objections, and we should strive to accommodate their requests. If coordination proves truly unfeasible, the reasons for being unable to adjust should be explained to them. Provided it falls within their rules or standards, the other party will typically cooperate to reach a mutually agreed-upon resolution or final decision.

In the electrical discipline, it is essential to understand CBOL (Civil, Building, and Other Landworks)-related matters, particularly concerning power lines. The electrical discipline is generally responsible for determining the locations and routes of cables, transformers, or electrical rooms in substations. However, many CBOL tasks—such as excavation, backfilling, and the installation of precast concrete foundations for transformers or substations—are typically performed by CBOL contractors.

As a contractor representing the owner, it is crucial to clearly delineate the scope of work with the utility company’s contractors. In North America, facilities outside the property line (redline) are usually designed and constructed by the utility company, while those inside the redline fall under the responsibility of the owner’s consulting firm or contractor. That said, the electrical department typically handles the supply and installation of BIT (Buried Interface Terminal) equipment, as well as the laying of primary and secondary feeders.

For electrical construction involving high-voltage systems (1,000 volts or 750 volts and above), special qualifications are required. Before selecting a contractor, approval from the electrical department must be obtained, as they enforce a prequalification process and only endorse contractors meeting their criteria.

Additionally, coordination with utility companies handling communications must be considered.

This section is relatively straightforward and does not involve service scale issues. As electrical consultants, our primary focus is on pipeline specifications, including conduit diameters and the methods of overhead or underground cable entry. Additionally, it is necessary to clarify the location of the communication equipment room, the routing of cables (such as path selection), and the coordination requirements between communication and civil engineering scopes, which are largely consistent with the collaboration methods used with power companies.

The communication entry section typically requires telecommunication companies to define backboard size specifications, entry power supply, and specific grounding requirements. Unlike power departments, communication lines must not only be brought in but also include wiring for each residential unit. From the entry point to individual household wiring, telecommunication companies in North America are responsible for determining and implementing conduit work. As electrical consultants, our primary responsibilities involve pipeline design, planning cable installation conditions, reserving space for equipment, and designing pre-buried conduits. Final wiring, termination, and commissioning are managed entirely by telecommunication companies.

Coordination with regulatory authorities, though involving minimal content, is equally important.

During the design process, the FARM system design must be coordinated with local fire departments, primarily reflected in the drawing review stage of the design phase. The fire department’s review is based on the FAR Code or Building Code, where the Building Code is reviewed by municipal authorities, and the FAR Code is reviewed by the fire department. After approval, the FAR Code may intervene during the implementation phase. If the fire department raises comments, modifications must be made according to their requirements, provided the comments are correct. If the comments are incorrect, explanations can be given, as some fire department personnel may lack sufficient experience and propose inaccurate feedback.

Building permit application and approval are mandatory processes for overseas projects. Each new project must obtain a building permit issued by the municipal construction development department. This department reviews the submitted technical drawings based on the Building Code. If comments are raised, the design must ensure compliance with the regulations and incorporate the feedback.

Streetlight design is managed by municipal authorities, with specific requirements varying by region. In North America, detailed design requirements must be obtained from the municipal department and applied to the design. The municipal department may propose modifications.

Coordination and collaboration between various disciplines is a key focus of the work. It primarily involves collaboration with the mechanical engineering discipline, which is our most frequent area of cooperation; coordination with the architectural discipline is also relatively frequent; while collaboration with the structural and civil landscape disciplines occurs less often.

Additionally, there are some special projects that require coordination with other disciplines, such as special design requirements like process or program design. If anyone has any questions about the previous content, you can raise them after the break, and we will address them at that time.

This is RFI versus RFI.

RFI is a communication document between contractors and consultants, while SI is an instruction provided by consultants, with different natures. SI is issued by consultants, whereas RFI originates from contractors.

This phase is referred to as “site clarification request”, meaning the design is finalized and the project has moved into the construction stage, hence the term “site”.

Whether it’s during the design phase or other stages, these are all considered technical issues. The so-called R5 refers to situations where the design phase has been completed. In reality, there are multiple types of R5:

Issues raised by the client during the design phase are called R5;

During the bidding phase, if modifications, additions, or scope adjustments are required, an SCISCR should be submitted immediately, explaining the necessity of the change. Once submitted, the owner or consultant will respond.

In the change request, it must be clearly stated: “This is not our original scope. There could be some additional scope.” If the other party acknowledges the change, then clarify: “Since this change is going to happen, which is not within our original scope, a change order will be sent for your approval after cost assessment.”

This B3RS standing is not within our original scope. This is additional scope for us. We will provide cost for this additional scope for your approval.

It is important to note that the contractor has no authority to make unilateral changes. An RFI must be submitted first. Only after confirmation from the other party can a formal change order be issued, becoming part of the contract.

In North America, if no change order is received, we will suspend subsequent work. The aforementioned content is for theoretical discussion only, and the actual implementation is your responsibility, which has caused you significant economic losses.
